assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, Ye's realisation and systematic-uncertainty record) opened the 1e-18 fractional-uncertainty regime, redefining what atomic spectroscopy can do and enabling tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a prospective redefinition of the second. Original, clear, and lastingly important.
assessment.attribution: Katori conceived the magic-wavelength lattice trapping idea and demonstrated early Sr clocks; Ye drove the most precise implementations and applications. A two-person prize is natural. Others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat groups) contributed to the field but the supplied credit supports a clean allocation.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs worldwide (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) confirm performance; interpretation is stable and the field is mature. Timing is well suited: the Hall/Hänsch comb prize is 2005 and the Wineland/Haroche prize 2012, so this is the natural next step in precision atomic physics.
uncertainties: Whether the intellectual priority of the lattice-clock idea should be shared more broadly (e.g. with early Sr-clock groups) is not settled by the supplied credit.
Technical overlap with the Ye group's comb and cavity work already recognised in earlier prizes could be argued by some.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provided the architecture (strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a microwave resonator, dispersive readout, two-qubit gates) on which most superconducting quantum processors are built. It transposed cavity QED into a solid-state, engineerable platform with high originality and enormous downstream impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf (2004) proposed it and Wallraff et al. demonstrated strong coupling in the same year; Schoelkopf's Yale group developed the transmon-era toolbox. Blais (theory), Wallraff (first experiment) and Schoelkopf (experimental development) are a defensible trio, though Girvin and Devoret are conspicuous omissions from the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced and extended by many groups for two decades; the interpretation is stable. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in circuits, so cQED is a natural but not strictly independent follow-up, and timing could be argued either way.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize (Devoret is a central figure in circuit-QED developments) may make the committee prefer waiting.
Girvin's role in the 2004 theory is not captured in the supplied names and the allocation of credit among theory and experiment is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube's observation of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos (2013) and the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 associations opened neutrino astronomy at TeV-PeV energies. A discovery of a new window on the universe, with clear lasting scientific impact.
assessment.attribution: Halzen was the principal driver of the concept and the collaboration's scientific leadership; Karle played a central role in detector construction and the analysis; Spiering is credited for early AMANDA/IceCube leadership but is omitted from my proposed pair. A fair prize would likely recognise the founder and one instrumental leader; collaboration-wide credit remains awkward.
assessment.maturity: Diffuse flux is established at many sigma and the TXS and NGC 1068 results are supported by multi-messenger follow-up, though source identification remains incomplete. Recognition is timely given the 2002 Koshiba/Davis prize precedent.
uncertainties: The pairing among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is not decisive from the supplied text and I cannot independently verify the internal history of the collaboration.
The astrophysical sources of most of the flux are still not identified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators created a new classification of electronic matter, with robust helical edge/surface states, and influenced condensed matter, photonics and quantum materials broadly. Original and conceptually clear, with massive impact.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele provided the theory (Z2 invariant, quantum spin Hall proposal in graphene); Molenkamp's group observed the HgTe quantum spin Hall edge transport. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (theory of HgTe) and Hasan/Moore/Balents/Fu contributions on three-dimensional TIs are outside this credit and complicate fairness.
assessment.maturity: Many independent experiments (HgTe, Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3 ARPES) confirm the picture; the field is mature and the idea has been recognised indirectly by the 2016 topological-phase prize.
uncertainties: Zhang's death and the BHZ HgTe proposal, plus the 3D TI contributions (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hasan), make the credit difficult.
The 2016 prize partially covers topological matter, so the committee may regard this as overlap.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of Hubbard-type models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (Mott insulator transition, single-site imaging, fermionic and bosonic implementations) provides controllable many-body quantum systems and is a cornerstone of atomic quantum simulation. As an atomic-physics theorist I value the clean connection between microscopic Hamiltonians and observed phases.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation; Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition and subsequently developed quantum-gas microscopes and fermionic simulations. Esslinger (fermionic Hubbard) is not in my proposed trio but is also strong; the supplied credit does not make the three-person limit simple.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature, replicated by many groups, and has produced quantitative benchmarks against theory. Quantum-gas prizes (2001, 1997) are older, so recognition is timely, although a major quantum-simulation breakthrough (e.g. solving an open problem) is still awaited.
uncertainties: Which of Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger and Zoller is most decisive, and whether Jaksch (not in the supplied credit) deserves recognition, is unresolved.
Scientific payoff for solving open Hubbard questions remains partially realised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light, from Caves's 1981 proposal for interferometric noise reduction to Kimble's early squeezing experiments and the implementation in gravitational-wave detectors, is a clear quantum-optics advance with direct large-scale application in LIGO/Virgo.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the key theory, Kimble the pioneering experimental squeezing demonstration, and Schnabel led the implementation for GEO600 and detector development. Slusher, Walls, Wu, Mavalvala and others are significant but not allocated in this three-name selection.
assessment.maturity: Squeezing is now operational in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 and the benefit is verified in the data; interpretation is stable. The 2017 gravitational-wave prize recognised the observation, not the quantum enhancement, so timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Credit is diffuse among Slusher, Walls, Wu, Kimble and the detector teams, making a three-person prize fragile.
The B040 candidate overlaps on Kimble and Schnabel with a different emphasis.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moiré engineering: flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in an exceptionally tunable platform. The 2011 flat-band prediction and the 2018 experiments launched a major new field.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat band at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group reported correlated insulator and superconducting phases with Cao and collaborators (junior researchers are not eligible within the three-person limit). The theory-experiment pairing is clear.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by multiple groups and extended to many moiré systems, but the nature of superconductivity and correlated states is still under active debate, which makes the interpretation less settled than for the others.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity in the moiré system remains unresolved.
Others (Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Dean, Kim; Yacoby) also contributed to twistronics, and it may be early.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade and programmable neutral-atom arrays provide a route to strongly interacting quantum simulators and gate-based quantum computers, building on the Jaksch-Zoller-Lukin proposals and subsequent experiments on controlled entanglement and tweezer arrays. It is close to my expertise in atomic structure and strongly excited atoms.
assessment.attribution: Lukin led the proposal and large-scale array experiments; Saffman and Browaeys gave key blockade experiments and gate demonstrations. Jaksch and Zoller (not eligible in this credit) were central to the original blockade gate proposal, and the credit allocation is therefore not obviously fair.
assessment.maturity: The field is still developing quickly with demonstrations of error-corrected-like operations, so the lasting scientific interpretation is partially unsettled; recognition may be slightly premature relative to the older candidates.
uncertainties: Missing credit for Jaksch and Zoller, and the importance of Weiss, Ahn, Bernien and others, complicates attribution.
Long-term impact on quantum computation is not yet fully established.
